extracted.intended_audience: authors submitting manuscripts to medical journals (and journal editors/reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and formatting manuscripts reporting medical research for submission to medical journals, covering structure (IMRAD), reporting guidelines, section-by-section content, ethics, statistics, and formatting/metadata requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: IMRAD structure and sectioning
rubrics_metrics.description: The text of articles reporting original research is usually divided into Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion (IMRAD).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IMRAD reflects scientific discovery; use subheadings within sections as needed. Other article types (meta-analyses, case reports, narrative reviews, editorials) may require different or less-structured formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplementary electronic material submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplementary electronic-only material should be submitted and sent for peer review simultaneously with the primary manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electronic formats allow layering, cross-linking, and extraction of portions of articles; supplementary files should be available to reviewers at submission so they can assess the full work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow reporting guidelines appropriate to study design
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors are encouraged to follow study-design–specific reporting guidelines (e.g., CONSORT for randomized trials, STROBE for observational studies, PRISMA for systematic reviews, STARD for diagnostic accuracy studies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should ask authors to follow these because they help describe studies in enough detail for evaluation. Authors of review manuscripts must describe methods for locating/selecting/extracting/synthesizing data (mandatory for systematic reviews). Use EQUATOR Network and NLM resources; follow SAGER for sex and gender reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article title content and retrieval
rubrics_metrics.description: The title should provide a distilled description of the complete article and include information that, along with the abstract, makes electronic retrieval sensitive and specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting guidelines recommend and some journals require inclusion of study design in the title (important for randomized trials and systematic reviews). Some journals require a short title entry (often ≤40 characters); electronic submission systems may limit title length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title page — author information and identifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Title page usually includes article title, author information, disclaimers, sources of support, word count, and sometimes number of tables/figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List each author's highest academic degrees (if journal publishes them), departmental and institutional affiliations, and full contact information for submission systems; include corresponding author's telephone and e-mail. ICMJE encourages listing authors' ORCID identifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimers
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclaimers (e.g., the views expressed are the author's and not the institution's) should be included where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear disclaimers on the title page when needed to clarify institutional positions vs author views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of support (funding) reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: List grants, equipment, drugs, and other support that facilitated the work or writing of the article; do not list sources/affiliations that did not contribute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funding sources and affiliations that have not contributed should not be listed, as that would be misleading. Distinguish direct support of the work from general institutional support for an author's time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word count reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a word count for the paper's text (excluding abstract, acknowledgments, tables, figure legends, and references) and a separate word count for the abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Word counts help editors and reviewers assess whether the information warrants the paper's length and whether the manuscript fits journal limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of figures and tables reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate the number of figures and tables, if required by submission systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These counts allow staff and reviewers to confirm inclusion of files and to assess whether the figures/tables warrant the manuscript's length and fit within journal space limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of relationships and activities (conflicts of interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure information for each author must be part of the manuscript; journals should develop standards for form and placement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ICMJE developed a uniform Disclosure Form and encourages adoption; editors may require disclosure on the title page or a separate manuscript section so reviewers/readers need not read individual forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract structure and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Original research, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses require structured abstracts that provide context/background, study purpose, basic procedures, main findings (with specific effect sizes and statistical/clinical significance when possible), principal conclusions, and limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstracts should emphasize new and important aspects and not overinterpret findings. Format required for structured abstracts differs by journal. Clinical trial abstracts should include items CONSORT identifies as essential. Because many databases index only the abstract, ensure it accurately reflects the article. Funding should be listed separately after the abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical trial registration and data identifiers in abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should publish the clinical trial registration number at the end of the abstract; when a registration number exists, list it when first using a trial acronym.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If data are deposited in a public repository or used in secondary analysis, state the unique persistent dataset identifier, repository name and number at the end of the abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction — scope and citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide context/background (nature of problem and its significance) and state the specific purpose, research objective, or hypothesis. Cite only directly pertinent references; do not include data or conclusions from the work being reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep citations focused and avoid reporting study data or conclusions in the introduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods — clarity and reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods should clearly explain how and why a study was done, with sufficient detail that others with access to the data could reproduce the results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include only information available at the time the plan/protocol was written; information obtained during the study belongs in Results. If an organization was contracted to help (data collection/management), detail that role in Methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics approval and adherence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Methods section should include a statement indicating research approval by an independent review body (e.g., ethics committee/IRB).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If doubt exists about adherence to the Helsinki Declaration, explain the rationale and demonstrate explicit approval of doubtful aspects by the review body (see ICMJE section II.E).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting authors' use of AI in conducting study
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors who used AI technology to conduct the study should describe its use in Methods in sufficient detail to enable replication, including tool used, version, and prompts where applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide enough detail so others can reproduce the AI-assisted approach; describe role of AI in data collection/analysis if applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and description of participants
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly describe selection of participants (including eligibility and exclusion criteria) and the source population; provide descriptive data for demographic variables and comment on representativeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for inclusion of representative populations; report sex/gender correctly (sex = biological; gender = identity/psychosocial), report sex/gender of participants/animals/cells unless inappropriate, define how race/ethnicity was determined and justify relevance, and use neutral, precise language that avoids stigmatizing terms. If study includes an exclusive population (e.g., only one sex), justify why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data collection, measurements, and materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify primary and secondary objectives (outcomes); identify methods, equipment (manufacturer name and address), and procedures in sufficient detail for reproduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference established methods (with pages) and briefly describe less-known methods; describe new or modified methods, give reasons and evaluate limitations. Identify drugs and chemicals (generic names, doses, routes) and appropriate scientific/gene names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical methods and reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe statistical methods in enough detail for a knowledgeable reader to judge appropriateness and verify reported results; quantify findings with appropriate indicators of error/uncertainty (e.g., confidence intervals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying solely on p-values; reference standard works for design/statistical methods; define statistical terms/abbreviations/symbols; specify statistical software and versions; distinguish prespecified analyses from exploratory analyses, including subgroups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Results — organization and completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Present results in logical sequence with main findings first; provide data on all primary and secondary outcomes identified in Methods; summarize rather than repeat table/figure data in text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place extra technical details in appendices or electronic supplements; give numeric results as both derivatives (percentages) and absolute numbers; restrict tables/figures to those needed to explain the argument; use graphs instead of large tables; do not duplicate data in graphs and tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of statistical terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid nontechnical uses of statistical terms (e.g., 'random', 'normal', 'significant', 'correlations', 'sample').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise statistical language to avoid misleading readers about study design or results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting by demographic variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate reporting of data by demographic variables (e.g., age and sex) should be routine to facilitate pooling across studies, unless compelling reasons not to stratify are given and explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide subgroup reporting to enable meta-analysis and interpretation of variable effects; if not stratifying, justify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion — content and caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin by briefly summarizing main findings; explore mechanisms or explanations; emphasize new/important aspects and place findings in context of relevant evidence; state limitations and implications for future research, clinical practice, or policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss influence of variables like sex/gender where appropriate; avoid repeating detailed data from other sections; link conclusions to study goals, avoid unqualified statements not supported by data; distinguish clinical from statistical significance; avoid economic claims unless supported by data; avoid claiming priority or alluding to incomplete work; state new hypotheses clearly labeled.

rubrics_metrics.name: References — selection and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide direct references to original research whenever possible; cite published articles rather than abstracts when possible; avoid citing predatory or pseudo-journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When citing preprints, indicate clearly they are preprints. References to 'in press' work should be designated so; 'unpublished observations' should be cited in text with written permission. Authors are responsible for accurate citations and should verify references (e.g., via PubMed) and ensure cited works are not retracted except when discussing the retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: References — format and numbering
rubrics_metrics.description: References should be numbered consecutively in the order first mentioned; identify references by Arabic numerals in parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Titles of journals should be abbreviated per MEDLINE/NLM; follow NLM’s Sample References and Citing Medicine for style and format; journals may vary on citing electronic references—consult the target journal's instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data and dataset identifiers in references
rubrics_metrics.description: Published articles should reference the unique persistent identifiers of datasets employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include dataset identifiers to facilitate data discovery and reuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal communications and AI-generated materials as sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid citing personal communications unless essential (with name and date) and obtain written permission; referencing AI-generated material as the primary source is not acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal communications require written permission and confirmation of accuracy; AI-generated content should not be treated as primary citable source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tables — design and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare tables per specific journal requirements; number consecutively and supply short self-explanatory titles; cite each table in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give short/abbreviated column headings; place explanatory matter in footnotes (not headings); explain nonstandard abbreviations in footnotes; use symbols consistently and identify statistical measures of variation (SD, SEM). Additional large backup tables may be published electronically or deposited—notify readers where available and submit them with the paper for peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures/illustrations — quality and legends
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit digital images in a suitable format and quality for print; figures should be self-explanatory with titles and detailed explanations in legends (legends on separate page).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For radiological/diagnostic images and photomicrographs provide high-resolution files; blots may require deposition of original photographs; labels (letters/numbers/symbols) should be clear/consistent and legible when reduced; photomicrographs should include internal scale markers and staining method; obtain permission and acknowledge original sources for previously published figures; identify and explain symbols/arrows/letters in legends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Units of measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Report measurements in metric units (meter, kilogram, liter) or decimal multiples; temperatures in degrees Celsius; blood pressures in mmHg unless otherwise required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report laboratory values in local units and SI units; consult target journal for preferred units and provide alternatives in parentheses if appropriate; editors may ask authors to add alternative or non-SI units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations and symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Use only standard abbreviations; avoid abbreviations in the title; spell out the term followed by the abbreviation in parentheses on first mention unless the abbreviation is a standard unit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid nonstandard abbreviations which can confuse readers; explain any symbols or nonstandard terms in footnotes or legends.
